about.bio:
Dean — The Engineer of the Last Order
“He knew exactly what he wanted. The house knew exactly what he feared.”

Dean was raised beneath the California sun, the son of Filipino parents and a boy whose childhood revolved around a blue Mini Cooper decorated with white racing stripes.

To most people, the vehicle was simply a car.

To Dean, it represented freedom.

But every time the Mini Cooper passed one particular establishment, Dean felt a strange uneasiness.

Seaside Donuts.

Nobody understood his hatred of the place.

The building was ordinary, its windows brightly lit and its shelves filled with pastries.

Yet Dean refused to enter.

He would cross the street to avoid it.

He would change routes to avoid passing it.

And whenever someone suggested buying donuts there, he would immediately refuse.

His friends assumed he was simply being picky.

They were only partially correct.

When Dean was twelve, he had entered Seaside Donuts with his family.

Inside, he noticed something peculiar.

Every customer was eating the same donut.

Every employee was smiling.

And the clock above the register was moving backward.

A cashier approached him.

"Welcome back, Dean."

He had never been there before.

The cashier handed him a receipt.

ORDER #0001

ITEM: ONE SECOND CHANCE

PRICE: YOUR FUTURE

When Dean looked up, every customer had turned toward him.

Their mouths were open.

But no sound came out.

He ran.

Three hours later, he was found sitting inside the family's Mini Cooper.

The engine was running.

The doors were locked.

And the radio was playing a recording of Dean screaming.

Years later, Dean became a black belt in taekwondo, developing remarkable discipline and precision.

He eventually enrolled at Seattle University to study electrical engineering, where he became known for his dedication to programming.

His supervisor, Dr. Louie, recognized his abilities and entrusted him with increasingly complicated projects.

Dean also became the lead electric guitarist for Bandwidth, bringing the same discipline and precision to music that he applied to engineering.

Every riff was deliberate.

Every solo calculated.

And every mistake unacceptable.

Dean approached guitar solos the same way he approached programming.

There was always a correct sequence.

Always an optimal solution.

And absolutely no room for unnecessary improvisation.

One night, while practicing a particularly difficult solo, Dean noticed his amplifier producing notes he had not played.

At first, he assumed it was electrical interference.

Then he realized the amplifier was playing the solo backward.

He recorded the sound and analyzed the waveform.

Hidden within the reversed audio was a voice.

"Your order is ready."

Dean froze.

It was the cashier from Seaside Donuts.

The following morning, he discovered that his guitar strings had somehow been replaced with thin strands of blue and white material, matching the racing stripes of his childhood Mini Cooper.

And taped to the guitar's body was a Subway receipt.

The order contained only one item.

FOOTLONG — FINAL MEAL.

Dean immediately threw the receipt away.

Three hours later, it appeared inside his guitar case.

His supervisor, Dr. Louie, eventually entrusted him with a particularly unusual project.

Dr. Louie handed Dean a flash drive containing a single file.

DO_NOT_RUN.exe

Naturally, Dean ran it.

His computer screen turned black.

A message appeared.

"WELCOME BACK, ORDER #0001."

Then his webcam activated.

On the screen, Dean saw himself sitting in front of the computer.

Except the other Dean was smiling.

And behind him stood the cashier from Seaside Donuts.

Dean slammed the laptop shut.

When he opened it again, the file had disappeared.

Only a new folder remained.

SUBWAY

Dean had always been extremely particular about food. He disliked unexpected ingredients, strange textures, and meals that failed to meet his exact preferences.

Subway was his sanctuary.

There, he could control every detail.

The bread.

The meat.

The vegetables.

The sauces.

Everything had an order.

Until one afternoon, when he entered his usual Subway location.

The employee greeted him by name.

"Your usual, Dean?"

He nodded.

The employee began preparing his sandwich.

But instead of bread, she placed a folded Seaside Donuts receipt on the counter.

"I'm sorry," she said.

"We're out of second chances."

The lights went out.

When they returned, Dean was standing alone in an abandoned restaurant.

The windows were boarded shut.

The sandwich in his hands was forty years old.

His darkest secret: Dean discovered that Dr. Louie had been researching Seaside Donuts long before Dean was born.

And hidden inside one of Dr. Louie's files was a photograph of the blue Mini Cooper.

Parked outside the donut shop.

Dated 1963.

On the passenger seat was a guitar case bearing the Bandwidth logo.

Andrew — The Craftsman of Hollow Souls
“He could create anything with his hands. Unfortunately, he never learned when to stop.”

Born from Chinese roots stretching back to Hong Kong, Andrew's heart had always belonged to the warm shores of Hawaii.

He was a man of endless energy. He danced as though possessed by music only he could hear, befriended strangers without hesitation, and spoke with enough enthusiasm to wake the dead.

But beneath his cheerful exterior lived an obsession.

Creation.

At Seattle University's Innovation Lab, Andrew became something of a legend. Students whispered about his supernatural ability to transform anything into something extraordinary.

He could sew clothing from scraps, construct intricate machines, manipulate 3D printers with terrifying precision, and create objects that seemed almost alive.

They called him The God of the Makerspace.

And like all gods, Andrew eventually became dissatisfied with what he had created.

His first mistake was a mannequin.

He had sewn it a beautiful outfit, carefully stitching every seam by hand. But when he returned the following morning, the mannequin was standing in a different position.

Its head was turned toward the door.

Its clothing was damp.

And beneath its fabric chest, something was beating.

Andrew laughed it off. After all, he had always been the extroverted type, the kind of person who could find humor in anything.

Until the mannequin began laughing back.

Among his countless creative pursuits, Andrew had dedicated nearly ten years of his life to mastering the trumpet.

When he joined Bandwidth, his enthusiasm was unmatched.

He danced during rehearsals, experimented with melodies, and occasionally played so loudly that the other members struggled to hear themselves.

Andrew believed that every song could be improved with a trumpet solo.

The rest of Bandwidth did not always share this belief.

Eventually, after a series of discussions, the band made the difficult decision to part ways with their beloved brass player.

The official explanation was that the band's musical direction no longer required trumpet.

The unofficial explanation was that Andrew had discovered approximately seventeen different ways to play over Dean's guitar solos.

Andrew took the news surprisingly well.

"That's okay. I'll just build my own band."

Everyone laughed.

Andrew laughed too.

Three days later, the Makerspace's 3D printers began operating without supervision.

They produced six small figurines.

Each resembled a member of Bandwidth.

Faith held a microphone.

JR sat behind a drum kit.

Dean carried an electric guitar.

Cliff held another guitar.

Edrich carried a bass.

And Andrew stood in the center with his trumpet.

At first, Andrew thought the figurines were adorable.

Then he noticed that the other five figurines were facing him.

Every morning, they moved slightly closer.

One evening, Andrew returned to find a seventh figurine.

It was a tiny wooden coffin.

Inside was a miniature trumpet.

Attached was a note:

"YOU HAVE BEEN REPLACED."

Andrew stared at the message.

Then shrugged.

"Honestly, the craftsmanship is pretty good."

Andrew buried himself in work. He took every paid opportunity he could find, refusing to sleep until his projects were completed. His friends joked that he would sell his own soul for twenty dollars.

One evening, he received a mysterious commission.

PAYMENT: $1,000,000

PROJECT: CONSTRUCT A VESSEL.

REQUIREMENT: IT MUST BE CAPABLE OF CARRYING THE DEAD.

Andrew immediately began building a boat.

No one knew who commissioned it. No one understood why its wooden hull occasionally bled when sanded.

But Andrew kept building.

His girlfriend, Ella, noticed something strange during their nightly Minecraft sessions. Every world they created eventually developed the same structure.

A massive wooden boat.

Floating above an endless black ocean.

Inside the boat stood hundreds of villagers.

Every villager had Andrew's face.

One night, while Andrew practiced his trumpet, the instrument produced a note so low that every light in the Makerspace shattered.

His sewing machines started operating by themselves.

The 3D printers began producing human teeth.

And from inside the unfinished boat, something knocked three times.

Andrew approached the hull.

"Hello?" he called cheerfully.

A voice answered from within.

"You finally finished making room for us."

His darkest secret: Andrew has never actually seen the person who commissioned the boat. Yet every morning, another thousand dollars appears in his bank account, and another name appears carved into the hull.

The latest name is his own.

And beneath it, someone has carved the words:

"BANDWIDTH REUNION TOUR."

Faith — The Silent Matriarch
“She would protect every one of them. But no one would ever know what she was protecting them from.”

Faith was born into a loving family whose roots stretched across the ocean to Hong Kong, though her heart had always belonged to the cold, rain-soaked forests of Washington.

She was a quiet child, small in stature and difficult to read. While other children expressed their emotions freely, Faith preferred to observe from a distance, revealing little of what occupied her thoughts.

Even those closest to her struggled to understand what went on inside her mind.

She rarely complained.

Rarely explained herself.

And when she made a decision, there was almost nothing anyone could do to change it.

As a young girl, Faith dreamed of becoming an Olympic swimmer.

She spent countless mornings submerged in freezing pools, practicing until her muscles ached and her lungs burned. She possessed a quiet determination that often frightened her instructors.

When told to rest, she continued swimming.

When told she had reached her limit, she swam another lap.

And when asked why she pushed herself so relentlessly, she would simply reply:

"Because I want to."

But her Olympic dreams ended one winter evening.

During a routine practice, Faith noticed a woman standing motionless at the bottom of the deep end.

The woman's hair floated gently around her face.

Her eyes were open.

And she was smiling.

Faith stopped swimming.

For several seconds, she stared into the depths.

Then, without screaming or calling for help, she calmly climbed out of the pool, collected her belongings, and went home.

She never returned.

When her parents asked what happened, Faith simply said:

"I don't want to swim anymore."

No amount of encouragement could convince her otherwise.

What she never told them was that the woman beneath the water had been wearing her face.

And when Faith climbed out of the pool, her reflection had remained behind.

Years later, Faith enrolled at Seattle University to study electrical engineering.

Although she sometimes doubted her abilities, she approached her studies with relentless determination. She was not the loudest student, nor the most confident, but she possessed an extraordinary capacity to endure challenges without complaint.

She became involved in numerous student organizations, assuming leadership positions that demanded patience, responsibility, and discipline.

She also remained an active member of her Chinese Christian church, finding comfort in her faith, family, and community.

Yet despite her responsibilities, Faith remained intensely private.

She rarely spoke about her personal struggles.

She did not seek attention.

And she never felt obligated to explain herself.

Her classmates eventually began calling her "The Mother of ECE."

Not because she was particularly affectionate or constantly hovering over everyone.

But because she cared in ways that were difficult to notice.

She remembered important details.

She offered help when it was needed.

She treated every friend with the same quiet consideration, never favoring one over another.

If someone needed assistance, Faith would help when she could.

If someone was struggling, she would listen.

But if someone asked her to do something she had already decided against, her answer was final.

"No."

"Come on, Faith."

"No."

"Please? Just this once?"

She would stare at them.

Silently.

Until they stopped asking.

Some joked that Faith's stubbornness was stronger than any force known to electrical engineering.

Others suspected it was something far older.

Despite her reserved personality, Faith possessed one unexpected talent.

She was the lead vocalist of Bandwidth, a student band formed by her closest friends at Seattle University.

Onstage, her quiet demeanor transformed into something extraordinary.

Her voice carried through crowded rooms with an almost supernatural clarity. She did not need extravagant gestures or dramatic movements to command attention.

She simply sang.

And people listened.

But even within the band, Faith remained a mystery.

She cared equally for every member, offering support without favoritism, but rarely revealing much about herself.

Cliff, one of the band's leaders, quickly learned that convincing Faith to perform a song she disliked was nearly impossible.

Dean could spend hours perfecting a guitar arrangement.

JR could insist that the song would sound incredible with his drums.

Andrew, back when he played trumpet for the band, could enthusiastically explain why it needed an extended brass solo.

Faith would listen to every argument.

Then calmly respond:

"I don't want to."

And that was the end of the discussion.

But during one late-night rehearsal, something unusual happened.

As Faith sang, the other musicians gradually stopped playing.

Not because she had made a mistake.

But because another voice had joined hers.

It was soft.

Beautiful.

Perfectly synchronized.

And unmistakably identical to her own.

Faith continued singing.

Cliff looked around the room.

JR lowered his drumsticks.

Dean unplugged his guitar.

The second voice continued.

When the song ended, everyone turned toward Faith.

"Did you hear that?" Cliff asked.

Faith nodded.

"What was it?"

She stared at the microphone.

"Nothing."

"Faith, that was definitely something."

She collected her belongings.

"I'm going home."

No one convinced her to stay.

Later that evening, Cliff examined the rehearsal recording.

Beneath Faith's vocals was another voice, singing in a language none of the band members recognized.

When he isolated the audio and reversed it, he heard a sentence repeated six times.

"SHE KNOWS WHAT IS COMING."

Faith never explained the incident.

And when Cliff asked her about it the following morning, she simply said:

"Don't play that recording again."

He laughed nervously.

"Why?"

Faith looked directly at him.

For the first time, her expression changed.

"Because I said so."

Several weeks later, Faith traveled to Canada to visit relatives.

Her family greeted her warmly, but something about their behavior seemed unusual.

They appeared surprised to see her.

"Faith? You're back already?"

She had not visited in months.

Her relatives insisted she had stayed with them the previous weekend.

They even showed her photographs.

In every picture, Faith was present.

But something was wrong.

In one photograph, she stood in the background, facing a wall.

In another, she sat at the dinner table, staring directly into the camera.

And in the final photograph, she was standing outside the house.

Even though the picture had been taken from the second floor.

Her family explained that during the previous visit, Faith had barely spoken.

She had spent most of her time silently observing everyone.

Occasionally, she would approach a family member and ask a strange question.

"Are you happy?"

If they answered yes, she would nod and walk away.

If they answered no, she would remain standing beside them.

For hours.

When her relatives asked why she behaved this way, she responded:

"I'm making sure everyone is okay."

That night, Faith examined the photographs alone.

She recognized the woman in them.

It was the same woman from the swimming pool.

The same woman who had sung alongside her during Bandwidth's rehearsal.

Faith quietly placed the photographs back into their envelope.

Then she turned off the lights.

From the bathroom came the sound of running water.

A familiar voice whispered:

"You can't protect all of them."

Faith stared into the darkness.

For a long moment, she said nothing.

Then she answered:

"I know."

The voice laughed.

"Then choose which one you love most."

Faith's expression remained unchanged.

"No."

The water stopped.

For the first time in decades, the thing beneath the surface had been refused.

And it did not know what to do.

Her darkest secret: Faith has been seeing the same woman in reflections for years. The woman claims that one day, Faith will be forced to sacrifice someone she loves to save the others.

But Faith refuses to choose.

Not Cliff.

Not JR.

Not Dean.

Not Andrew.

Not Edrich.

No one.

And every night, the woman grows more impatient.

Recently, Faith discovered a handwritten list beneath her pillow.

It contained the names of all her friends.

Beside each name was a date.

At the bottom was a final instruction:

"CHOOSE ONE, OR LOSE THEM ALL."

Faith read the message.

Folded the paper.

Placed it in a drawer.

And whispered:

"No."

Somewhere far beneath the waters of Washington, something ancient began to scream.

Because the house had finally encountered something it could not control.

A woman who had already made up her mind.

JR — The Alaskan Prodigy
“He could outrun anyone, outplay everyone, and catch anything. But something had been chasing him his entire life.”

Born to Filipino parents, JR grew up with an unusual fascination for Alaska.

While others dreamed of tropical beaches and warm weather, JR longed for frozen lakes, endless forests, and mountains that disappeared into the clouds.

From childhood, he was exceptionally athletic.

Basketball came naturally to him. He could shoot with either hand, confuse defenders with impossible movements, and perform feats of coordination that seemed almost supernatural.

His skills extended beyond the court.

He became a Division I track-and-field athlete, mastered complex yo-yo tricks, and developed an almost frightening talent for NBA 2K.

But his greatest passion was fishing.

JR could spend hours beside a frozen lake, patiently waiting for something to bite.

And something always did.

During one trip to Alaska, JR ventured farther into the wilderness than he ever had before.

He discovered a lake absent from every map.

The water was perfectly still.

No birds flew overhead.

No insects disturbed the surface.

Yet JR felt compelled to cast his line.

Almost immediately, something pulled.

He fought against it for hours, refusing to surrender.

Whatever was beneath the water possessed tremendous strength.

Eventually, JR pulled his catch toward the surface.

It was not a fish.

It was a human hand.

Pale. Frozen. Clutching a yo-yo.

And on its wrist was a bracelet identical to one JR had lost as a child.

He dropped the fishing rod and ran.

But when he returned to his cabin, the rod was waiting beside his bed.

Still dripping.

Since that day, JR's physical abilities have become increasingly unnatural.

He runs faster than he should.

His reflexes are impossibly sharp.

And during basketball games, he occasionally hears a voice whispering exactly where the ball will land.

At Seattle University, JR pursued computer engineering, becoming known as the dependable coder of the group.

His programs were efficient, his athletic achievements impressive, and his kindness genuine.

He had a loving girlfriend named Kayla, who believed she knew everything about him.

JR also became the drummer for Bandwidth, where his extraordinary coordination made him a natural behind the drum kit.

His powerful arms and lightning-fast reflexes allowed him to maintain rhythms that seemed impossible for an ordinary human.

His bandmates joked that being a Division I athlete had somehow made him a Division I drummer.

But one evening, while practicing alone, JR noticed something unusual.

Every time he struck the snare drum, he heard a second beat.

Not from the drum.

From beneath the floor.

He experimented with different rhythms.

Whatever was below copied them perfectly.

Then it began playing rhythms of its own.

JR followed along, fascinated by the strange exchange.

The tempo increased.

Faster.

Faster.

Until his hands were moving so quickly that his drumsticks began to splinter.

Suddenly, the mysterious drumming stopped.

A voice rose from beneath the floorboards.

"Your turn to follow."

That night, JR dreamed of the frozen Alaskan lake.

Only this time, instead of fishing, he was sitting behind his drum kit in the middle of the ice.

Something enormous was moving beneath him.

And with every beat of his bass drum, the ice cracked a little more.

Kayla soon began noticing disturbing behavior.

Sometimes, JR would stare at empty corners of a room, moving his fingers as though manipulating an invisible yo-yo.

Other times, he would wake in the middle of the night and begin practicing basketball shots without a ball.

One evening, Kayla found him standing in the kitchen.

His eyes were closed.

His right hand was extended.

And something invisible appeared to be pulling against his fingers.

"JR?"

He did not respond.

"What are you doing?"

His mouth moved slowly.

"Something's on the line."

Kayla looked down.

A thin fishing line extended from his fingertips, disappearing beneath the kitchen floor.

Suddenly, it tightened.

JR smiled.

"I think I caught something."

Then the floorboards began to bend upward.

Despite his extraordinary abilities, JR possessed two potentially fatal weaknesses: shellfish and tree nuts.

His friends often joked that a man capable of outrunning nearly anyone could still be defeated by a shrimp.

But the creature beneath the Alaskan lake seemed to know this.

Recently, JR began finding seashells in his shoes.

And every time he opened his backpack, there was another unopened bag of mixed nuts.

His darkest secret: JR has been receiving photographs from an unknown number. Each shows him standing beside the same frozen lake.

In every new photograph, the figure beneath the ice is closer to the surface.

And it looks more like him.

In the latest photograph, the figure is holding a pair of drumsticks.

Edrich — The Prodigy of Beautiful Chaos
“Some people bring order to chaos. Edrich brings chaos to order.”

Born to Filipino parents, Edrich's heart belonged to the tropical shores of Hawaii. But unlike the peaceful islands she adored, there was absolutely nothing peaceful about her.

From the moment she could speak, Edrich had been an unstoppable force of nature.

Loud. Energetic. Unpredictable.

She possessed no filter between her brain and her mouth. Whatever thought entered her head immediately became everyone else's problem.

She laughed at inappropriate moments, challenged people twice her age, and had an uncanny ability to turn an ordinary afternoon into a catastrophic event.

Despite being the youngest of her friends, Edrich was arguably the most terrifying.

Not because she was evil.

But because nobody could predict what she would do next.

Her extraordinary talent for robotics earned her recognition at an unusually young age. By her sophomore year at Seattle University, she had already secured an internship, and eventually her abilities attracted the attention of the Department of Defense.

What she worked on there remains classified.

Officially, her assignment involved advanced robotic systems.

Unofficially, three engineers resigned, an autonomous vehicle drove itself into the ocean, and an entire laboratory was placed under military quarantine.

When questioned about the incident, Edrich simply laughed.

"Oops."

No further explanation was provided.

Her friends had grown accustomed to her chaotic behavior. She would burst into rooms without warning, make outrageous declarations, and occasionally lean toward someone to whisper something deeply unsettling.

Then she would return to laughing as though nothing had happened.

Her boyfriend, Jason, loved her dearly.

He was also absolutely terrified of her.

On one occasion, Jason received a phone call from Edrich at 3:00 AM.

"Babe, quick question. Hypothetically, how hard is it to hide a robot?"

"What kind of robot?"

"A big one."

"How big?"

A metallic screech echoed through the phone.

"Never mind, I figured it out!"

The call ended.

Jason did not sleep that night.

Despite her terrifying unpredictability, Edrich had one weakness.

Mother Faith.

Faith was the only person capable of calming Edrich's relentless energy. Where others saw a walking disaster, Faith saw a younger sister who simply needed guidance.

Edrich could argue with professors, insult authority figures, and challenge anyone foolish enough to question her intelligence.

But if Faith told her to behave, she would reluctantly obey.

For approximately six minutes.

Although many of her closest friends performed in the Seattle University band Bandwidth, Edrich had never officially been a member.

She had never attended their rehearsals or performed alongside them. Her musical experience was limited, but she had recently developed an interest in learning the bass guitar.

There was, however, one condition.

Cliff had to teach her.

Cliff, one of Bandwidth's guitarists and leaders, had spent years teaching others how to build machines and play instruments. Teaching Edrich seemed like a reasonable challenge.

But Cliff had no idea what he was agreeing to.

One afternoon, Edrich approached him with an unusually enthusiastic proposition.

"Cliff, teach me bass."

Cliff agreed, explaining that she would need patience, practice, and a basic understanding of rhythm.

Edrich stared at him.

"Okay, but how long until I'm better than you?"

Cliff laughed.

Edrich did not.

She had already begun researching the mechanical properties of bass strings, amplifier circuitry, and the frequencies capable of producing structural resonance.

Nobody knew why.

Cliff decided not to ask.

Although her lessons had not yet begun, Edrich had already developed ambitious plans for her future musical career.

She wanted to learn bass.

She wanted to become good at it.

And, if possible, she wanted to build a robotic bass player that could accompany her.

One evening, Cliff received a message from Edrich.

"Hey, random question. Can a bass guitar kill someone?"

He replied that ordinary bass guitars were not designed to do that.

Three minutes later, she responded:

"Okay, so theoretically..."

Cliff turned off his phone.

But something changed after Edrich's latest robotics project.

She had constructed a small autonomous machine capable of navigating complex environments without human assistance.

One evening, the robot began behaving strangely.

It followed Edrich everywhere.

It copied her movements.

It even began imitating her laughter.

At first, she found this amusing.

Then it started laughing when she wasn't.

One night, Edrich woke to the sound of footsteps outside her bedroom.

She opened the door.

Her robot stood in the hallway.

Its mechanical head tilted sideways.

In a perfect imitation of her voice, it whispered:

"Hey, wanna see something funny?"

Behind it stood seventeen identical machines.

All laughing.

The following morning, Cliff received another message from Edrich.

"Hey, are you free to teach me bass today?"

Attached was a photograph.

It showed seventeen robots standing in perfect formation.

Each holding a bass guitar.

Cliff stared at the image.

Then another message appeared.

"Don't worry, they're beginners too."

Her darkest secret: Edrich never programmed her robots to reproduce. Yet every time she builds one, another appears the following morning.

Recently, they have stopped listening to her.

Except when she mentions Faith.

Then every machine turns toward her and asks the same question.

"WHERE IS MOTHER?"

And although Edrich has never played a single rehearsal with Bandwidth, Cliff recently discovered an old photograph of the band performing inside an unfamiliar mansion.

Standing behind them was Edrich.

Holding a bass guitar.

Smiling directly at the camera.

The photograph was dated twenty-seven years before she was born.
